title: Quantum 3-coloring of cycles in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) rounds
formal:
Does there exist one uniform quantum-LOCAL protocol \(A\) and a function \(T:\mathbb N_{\ge3}\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge3\) and every injective identifier assignment \(\lambda:V(C_n)\to\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), all nodes of the consistently oriented cycle \(C_n\) finish within \(T(n)\) communication rounds on every possible execution branch, and their classical outputs \(c_v\in\{1,2,3\}\) satisfy
\[
\Pr\bigl[\forall\{u,v\}\in E(C_n),\ c_u\ne c_v\bigr]\ge1-\frac1n,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{T(n)}{1+\log^{*}_2n}=0?
\]
The probability is over the protocol's quantum measurement outcomes. Initially the quantum state is a product of local zero states. Each node knows \(n\), its own identifier and the predecessor/successor ports, and communication in both directions is permitted.
definitions:
For specification only, \(C_n\) has vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1}\) and edges \(\{v_i,v_{(i+1)\bmod n}\}\). Its consistent orientation tells each node which port leads to its successor and which to its predecessor. The indices \(i\) are not inputs to the protocol. Identifiers are distinct integers in \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), represented in binary. Nodes receive no distinguished leader, numerical position, neighbor identifiers, list of all identifiers, or other global information beyond \(n\). The identifier assignment is fixed before quantum randomness; the success bound holds for every such assignment.

All nodes execute the same fixed finite classical control program. Its initial classical input consists only of \(n\), the node's identifier and its two port labels. Classical computation manipulates finite binary strings by ordinary Turing-machine operations and may determine which local qubits to use next. There is no bound on local computation time, local storage or message length, but every local phase and every message must be finite on every possible branch. No advice depending on \(n\), the identifiers or the graph is supplied.

Local quantum storage is a finite tensor product of qubits. A node may append a fresh qubit in state \(\lvert0\rangle\), discard a local qubit, apply \(H\) or \(T\) to one local qubit, apply CNOT to an ordered pair of distinct local qubits, or measure a local qubit in the computational basis, with subsequent classical control depending on the outcome. The gates are
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{\mathrm i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathrm{CNOT}\lvert x,y\rangle=\lvert x,x\mathbin{\oplus}y\rangle
\quad(x,y\in\{0,1\}).
\]
Here \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) and \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. On a global density operator \(\rho\), a local gate acts by unitary conjugation on its chosen registers; discarding a register takes its partial trace. A computational-basis measurement with outcome \(b\in\{0,1\}\) has probability \(\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\) and, when that probability is nonzero, leaves normalized state \(P_b\rho P_b/\operatorname{tr}(P_b\rho)\), where \(P_b\) projects the measured qubit onto \(\lvert b\rangle\). Classical random choices may be obtained by such measurements. There is no postselection that discards unsuccessful outcomes from the success probability.

A communication round consists of finite local processing followed by simultaneous noiseless transmission of finite quantum registers along the cycle edges. Each node may send registers to both neighbors and receives their sent registers before the next local phase. Sending transfers ownership of the qubits; it does not copy unknown states. Classical messages can be encoded as computational-basis registers. A final finite local phase may produce the node's color without another round. There is no communication between nonneighbors, no information conveyed by elapsed local computation time, and no additional inter-node channel. The initial global quantum state is the tensor product of all freshly initialized local \(\lvert0\rangle\) registers; there is no shared randomness or preshared entanglement. Entanglement created by the protocol through counted communication is allowed.

Every node must output one color and halt, including on branches where the resulting coloring is improper. A possible branch is one whose finite measurement outcomes have nonzero Born probability. The round bound holds on every such branch and uniformly over all identifier assignments of the same size, rather than merely in expectation or with high probability. Local operations, message lengths and numbers of qubits are not charged to round complexity. The program has no real-number oracle or arbitrary exact unitary as an extra primitive; the gate set above retains the card's existing concrete uniform interpretation.

For real \(x\ge1\), \(\log^{*}_2x\) is the least nonnegative integer \(r\) for which applying \(\log_2\) repeatedly \(r\) times reaches a value at most \(1\), stopping as soon as that occurs. The displayed limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(N\) such that \(T(n)\le\varepsilon(1+\log^{*}_2n)\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The probability target is global correctness of all edges simultaneously, not separate correctness probabilities for individual nodes.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a uniform protocol and a worst-case round-bound function satisfying every stated input, quantum-operation, termination and global-success condition, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of that existence statement. A conditional lower bound alone does not prove nonexistence. A lower bound limited to anonymous probability-one protocols, to one-way one-round communication, to two-coloring, or to growing-degree trees does not settle the stated protocol class.
why: Cycle coloring is a basic distributed symmetry-breaking problem with a sharp classical locality threshold. Settling whether quantum communication beats that threshold would establish a concrete capability or limitation for coordinating neighboring processors with classical outputs.

importance.reason: A central concrete benchmark for quantum distributed computation, with an elementary output condition and a sharp classical threshold. The recent zero-error breakthrough leaves the practically standard high-probability regime unresolved.

progress.text: Naor gives a classical randomized lower bound for distributed ring coloring.
Linial establishes the classical deterministic locality lower bound; the classical cycle-coloring complexity is \(\Theta(\log^{*}n)\).
Holroyd, Hutchcroft and Levy establish finitely dependent colorings of finite cycles.
The second rooted-tree/even-cycle revision distinguishes the growing-degree three-color result from bounded-degree cycles.
A preprint proves the anonymous probability-one lower bound and explicitly retains high-probability cycle coloring as open.
A preprint gives a high-probability lower bound for one-way one-round four-coloring, with the broader communication question still open.
Checked these model boundaries and made global success, quantum operations, uniformity and worst-case round accounting explicit.

context_blocks.text: The primary problem list asks whether cycles can be 3-colored in \(o(\log^{*}n)\) quantum rounds and separately asks about a constant-round algorithm. This card retains the first question with its already chosen orientation, identifiers, known size, finite gate set and global error bound.

Classical deterministic and high-probability randomized cycle coloring both have \(\Theta(\log^{*}n)\) round complexity. The August 2026 paper summarizes those classical bounds and distinguishes them from the unknown quantum-LOCAL complexity.

Finitely dependent proper color distributions exist on finite cycles: collections of colors on vertex sets at sufficiently large graph distance are independent. This is a statement about distributions, not an implementation by the local quantum protocol specified here. The finite-cycle result is due to Holroyd, Hutchcroft and Levy, following the earlier integer-line construction.

The July 2026 preprint proves quantum lower bounds for 3-coloring rooted trees using growing degree, and for 2-coloring even cycles. It explicitly distinguishes the bounded-degree case; neither result resolves three-coloring cycles.

The August 2026 preprint proves a linear-round lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that color cycles with probability exactly one. Its Section 1.4 leaves high-probability correctness open. The identified, nonzero-error model here is retained.

The September 2026 preprint rules out high-probability four-coloring in the restricted one-way one-round quantum model. Section 1.4 explicitly leaves bidirectional communication and additional rounds as further questions; this does not resolve the sub-log-star target.

The cited quantum papers allow general finite-dimensional local operations in their mathematical models. This card preserves its pre-existing uniform finite-gate formulation; the review does not claim an exact compilation equivalence for probability-one results.

sentences: Processors on an oriented cycle must choose three classical colors with different colors at every edge.
They may perform finite local quantum computations and communicate qubits with both neighbors in synchronous rounds.
One uniform protocol must work for every cycle size and every distinct identifier assignment, starting without shared randomness or entanglement.
The target is worst-case communication below the log-star scale with global success probability at least one minus one over the number of nodes.
Recent zero-error and one-way one-round lower bounds cover restricted models and do not resolve this high-probability question.
